Ha detto che era fiero di noi
You report what someone else said with reported speech (dice che…, chiede se…, mi dice di…), change pronouns and tenses, and review the subjunctive and pronouns.
Bellini says he's proud of us.
Pietro is asking if we're coming back in July.
He told me not to forget the brush.
Giulia replied that she was tired but happy.
To report a statement in the present: Dice che è stanco.
To report a question: Chiede se vieni. Chiede dove abiti.
To report an order or advice: Mi dice di aspettare.
To change pronouns and possessives: «Io sono felice» → Dice che lui è felice.
To report in the past: Ha detto che era stanco / che aveva finito / che sarebbe venuto.
To review the unit: the subjunctive, demonstrative and possessive pronouns.
June, the last week in Sibiu. Tomorrow the exhibition of the twelve restored paintings opens. Matei phones Graziella. Next to him, Giulia is reading an email from Bellini.
Hello, Matei! So, how's it going? Pietro is tugging at my sleeve: he wants to know everything.
Really well. The opening is tomorrow. And Bellini has just written.
(reading) He says he's arriving tonight on the plane from Bologna. He says he's seen the photos of the paintings and that he's proud of us.
Proud? Bellini wrote "proud"? Good Lord, the world must be ending!
And he's asking whether the portrait with the blue veil is ready for the exhibition.
And then… (laughs) he tells me to be on time for the ceremony. He wrote "on time" in capital letters.
Pietro is asking me to ask you something: he wants to know when you're coming back to Florence.
Tell him we're coming back on the thirtieth of June. And tell him I'm bringing the teddy bear he asked me for.
(in the distance) Pietro! They say they're coming back on the thirtieth and they're bringing you the bear! … He says he wants a big bear, not a small one.
Graziella, Matei's mother asked me to ask you for the ribollita recipe. She says she wants to cook it for Bellini.
Tell her I'll send it right away. And tell her that if Bellini doesn't finish it, it's because he's too moved!
The passato remoto of "dire" (in books): DIS-se, DIS-se-ro, with a double S. You'll meet it a lot in stories.
Review: DIGLI = "dee-lyee", GLIELA = "lye-la", with a soft GL.
Seven syllables: ee-now-goo-ra-TSYO-ne, with "tsyo" at the end.
Double PP, AU = a diphthong: ap-PLOW-so.
When the reporting verb is in the present (dice, chiede, risponde), the tense of the verb does NOT change. Only the person and the pronouns change:
Bellini dice che è fiero di noi.
Pietro dice che vuole un orso grande.
Giulia dice che ha finito il ritratto.
Matei dice che torneranno il trenta.
Don't forget to change the pronouns: «io» → lui / lei, «mio» → suo, «voi» → noi (if they're talking to us).
Yes / no questions are reported with SE. Questions with a question word keep the word (dove, quando, perché, che cosa, chi):
Chiede se il ritratto è pronto.
In careful style, the subjunctive can follow "chiedere se": "Mi chiede se io sia pronto." In speech, the indicative is normal.
3. Orders and advice: DIRE DI + infinitive
Mi dice di arrivare in orario.
Mi ha detto di non dimenticare il pennello.
Mi ha detto di chiedere la ricetta a Graziella.
As in Romanian: "Mi-a spus SĂ ajung la timp" = "Mi ha detto DI arrivare in orario".
When the reporting verb is in the past (ha detto, disse), the tenses "take a step back":
"Ha detto che sarebbe venuto" (past conditional) is the correct form for a future in the past — NOT "che verrebbe". Learn it as a block; we'll study it at B1.
Voglio che vi sposiate a Sorrento.

Benché non parli italiano, si fa capire.

Che cosa dice Bellini a Giulia?
Che cosa vuole Doina da Graziella?

The great hall of the Brukenthal Museum was full. There were the mayor, the Italian ambassador, journalists from three TV channels, the workshop colleagues, Doina and Ion dressed as if for a wedding, and Ilinca, who was holding hands with a tall young man in glasses. Nobody yet knew who he was.

Giulia had arrived an hour early. When Bellini saw her, he looked at his watch, then at her, then at his watch again. "Miss Esposito," he said, "I've seen many miracles in my life. This is the greatest."

The director, Mrs Popescu, gave the first speech. She said the collaboration between Florence and Sibiu had been an extraordinary success. She explained that the twelve paintings had come to Sibiu two centuries ago, in Baron Brukenthal's collection, and that some had never been restored.

Then Bellini spoke. He said he didn't like making speeches and that he would speak briefly. He spoke for forty minutes. He talked about the Florence flood, about his grandfather Ernesto, about the tiny brush and the letter found behind the Madonna. He said that Madonna was now there, in Sibiu, next to the twelve paintings, and that his grandfather's letter was on display under glass beside her.

At the end he looked at Matei and Giulia in the front row. He said that in forty years of work he had had many assistants, but none had ever treated paintings like children, the way the two of them did. He said his grandfather would have been happy to meet them. Then he stopped, because he couldn't speak any more.

The audience applauded for two minutes. Doina was crying. Ion, who hadn't understood a word of Italian, clapped louder than anyone. Mrs Popescu was wiping her eyes too. Later she told the journalists that in thirty years of work she had never seen an Italian professor cry in public, and that it had been wonderful.

Then came the moment of the portrait. Matei and Giulia removed the white cloth together. Underneath was the woman with the blue veil, free at last of the nineteenth-century overpainting. Her face was luminous, her brown eyes looked at the audience with a kind of smile.

A journalist came up to Doina with a microphone. She asked her what she thought of the portrait. Doina answered, in Romanian, that she didn't know much about art. But she said the woman had her mother's eyes, and that she felt as if she were seeing her again after thirty years.
Giulia looked at Matei. "I told you," she whispered. "On the first day, in January. I told you she had your mother's eyes."

That evening at dinner Ilinca stood up, glass in hand. She said she had an announcement. She introduced the young man in glasses: his name was Radu, he was a doctor, and he was her boyfriend. Ion looked at Radu for a very long moment. Then he poured two glasses of pălincă and gave him one. "Noroc," he said. Ilinca whispered to Giulia that this was her father's way of saying yes.

Later, on the phone, Pietro asked Matei to tell him everything. Matei told him that Bellini had spoken for forty minutes, that Mum had cried and that Ilinca had a boyfriend. "And the bear?" Pietro asked. Matei promised him it was already in the suitcase. A big one, not a small one.

Reading text: The Sibiu newspaper article
An article from the local paper (translated into Italian). Read and answer.
Yesterday the Brukenthal Museum opened the exhibition of the twelve restored Italian paintings.
Professor Bellini of the Uffizi said the collaboration will continue next year too.
The two restorers, a Romanian man and a Neapolitan woman, explained that they will get married in September.
The museum director asked them whether they will come back to Sibiu. They said yes: "Half our family is here."
